newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus slaps new tax on Ukraine imports.
newsitem.headline: Belarus slaps new tax on Ukraine imports.

text.p: Belarus imposed an import tax on goods from the neighbouring former Soviet republic of Ukraine on Friday, in a move likely to be seen as a friendly nod to Russia.
The decree, ordered by President Alexander Lukashenko, imposes a value added tax on Ukrainian goods from now, except on items produced as a result of cooperation beteween the countries.

The document, published in the official press, gave no details of the size of the tax but said the government had been ordered by Lukashenko to hold talks with the Ukrainian government on the subject.
It said representatives from Minsk's partners in a customs pact -- Russia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyztan -- should also take part in the negotiations.
The decree was connected to a decision by Ukraine to cancel value added tax on goods exported to Belarus, it said.
Ukrainian goods had been subject to customs duties like imports from other states outside the pact but not to value added tax.
The economy ministry put losses in excise duties on alcohol, wine and vodka imported from Ukraine at about $180 million last year.

International lending bodies have cut off loans to Belarus, where Lukashenko has taken a slow approach to reforms and drawn sharp criticism from the West especially since he won a referendum to expand his powers greatly in November.

Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma was the first leader to meet Lukashenko on home territory after the referendum, and the trip was taken as a sign Belarus was demonstrating to Russia that it had other partners on its doorstep.
Lukashenko had threatened to close the Ukrainian border because of accusations in Moscow that cheap vodka was flooding into the Russian market via Belarus.

But he then signed a deal with Kuchma which was meant to ease traffic across the border. Lukashenko has accused Russia of resisting closer ties since they formed a "Community of Sovereign Republics" in April.
He is due to meet Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Moscow on March 7 and a joint session of their parliaments is planned a few days after that to discuss union.

Yeltsin sent a letter to Lukashenko in January suggesting faster moves towards unification. The 42-year-old leader has issued conflicting signals on his desire for unity with Russia but has recently reiterated a desire for stronger economic ties.
